source_text: Τοσούτων ἀγαθῶν καὶ τηλικού των, ἄθλιε, προτιμοτέραν ἄγεις τὴν ἡδονήν; Νοῶ γάρ σου τὴν ὑπέρθεσιν, κἂν περιστέλλῃ τοῖς ῥήμασιν· αὐτὰ βοᾷ τὰ πράγματα, κἂν τῇ φωνῇ σιωπᾷς. Ἔασον, ἀποχρήσωμαι τῇ σαρκὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν τῶν αἰσχρῶν, ἐγκυλισθῶ τῷ βορβόρῳ τῶν ἡδονῶν, αἱμάξω τὰς χεῖρας, ἀφέλωμαι τὰ ἀλ λότρια, δολίως πορευθῶ, ἐπιορκήσω, ψεύσωμαι· καὶ τότε τὸ βάπτισμα, ὅταν λήξω ποτὲ τῶν κακῶν, ὑποδέξομαι. Εἰ μὲν οὖν καλὸν ἡ ἁμαρτία, φύλασσε ταύτην εἰς τέλος· εἰ δὲ βλαβερὰ τῷ ποιοῦντι, τί ἐπιμένεις τοῖς ὀλεθρίοις; Οὐδεὶς, χολὴν ἐμέσαι ζητῶν, ἐκ πονηρᾶς καὶ ἀκολάστου διαίτης πολυπλασίονα ταύτην ἑαυτῷ συναθροίζει. Καθαίρειν προσῆκε τῶν λυπούντων τὸ σῶμα, οὐ μέντοι κατασκευάζειν τὴν νόσον μείζονα τῆς δυνάμεως. Φαίνεται ἡ ναῦς μέχρι τίνος τὸ βάρος τῶν ἀγωγίμων ὑφίσταται, τὸ δὲ ὑπὲρ τοῦτο καταβαπτίζει. Φοβήθητι μὴ καὶ σὺ τὰ παραπλήσια πάθῃς, καὶ μείζονα τῆς ἀφέσεως ποιήσας τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, πρὸ τῶν ἐλπισθέντων λιμένων ὑποστῇς τὸ ναυάγιον. Οὐ βλέπει Θεὸς τὰ γινόμενα; ἢ οὐ νοεῖ σου τὰ ἐνθυμήματα; ἢ συνεργάζεταί σοι τὰς ἀνομίας; Ὑπέλαβες ἀνομίαν, φησὶν, ὅτι ἔσομαί σοι ὅμοιος. Σὺ δὲ, ἀνδρὸς μὲν θνη τοῦ φιλίαν πραγματευόμενος, δι' εὐεργεσίας αὐτὸν προσάγῃ, ἐκεῖνα λέγων καὶ πράττων οἷσπερ ἂν αἴσθῃ χαίροντα· Θεῷ δὲ προσοικειούμενος, καὶ εἰς τὴν υἱοῦ τάξιν ἐλπίζων παραδεχθήσεσθαι, τὰ ἐχθρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πράττων, καὶ διὰ τοῦ νόμου παραβάσεως ἀτιμάζων αὐτὸν, ἐξ ὧν μάλιστα προσκρούεις, ἐκ τούτων ἐλπίζεις τὴν οἰκειότητα; Ὅρα μὴ ἐπ' ἐλπίδι τῆς ἀπο λυτρώσεως, πλῆθος κακῶν σεαυτῷ συλλεξάμενος, τὴν μὲν ἁμαρτίαν συναθροίσῃς, τῆς δὲ συγχωρήσεως ἀποτύχῃς. Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται. Μὴ ἐμπορεύου τὴν χάριν. Μὴ εἴπῃς· Καλὸς μὲν ὁ νόμος, ἀλλ' ἡδίων ἡ ἁμαρτία. Ἡδονὴ ἄγκιστρόν ἐστι τοῦ διαβόλου πρὸς ἀπώλειαν ἕλκον. Ἡδονὴ μήτηρ τῆς ἁμαρτίας· ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία τὸ κέντρον ἐστὶ τοῦ θανάτου. Ἡδονὴ τροφὸς τοῦ αἰωνίου σκώληκος, ἣ πρὸς καιρὸν μὲν καταλεαίνει τὸν ἀπολαύοντα, ὕστερον δὲ πικροτέρας χολῆς ποιεῖται τὰς ἀναδόσεις. Οὐδὲν ἄλλο βοᾷ ἡ ὑπέρθεσις ἢ ταῦτα· βασιλευσάτω ἐν ἐμοὶ πρῶτον ἡ ἁμαρτία, εἶτα βασιλεύσει ποτὲ καὶ ὁ Κύριος. Παρα στήσω μου τὰ μέλη ὅπλα ἀδικίας τῇ ἀνομίᾳ· εἶτα παραστήσω ποτὲ καὶ ὅπλα δικαιοσύνης αὐτὰ τῷ Θεῷ. Οὕτω καὶ Κάϊν προσέφερε τὰς θυσίας· τὰ πρῶτα τῇ ἀπολαύσει τῇ ἑαυτοῦ, τὰ δεύτερα τῷ κτίσαντι καὶ δωρησαμένῳ Θεῷ. Ὅτε δυνατὸς εἶ ἐν ἔργοις, τὴν νεότητά σου ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις προσαναλίσκεις. Ὅτε ἀποκάμῃ τὰ ὄργανα, τότε προσάγεις αὐτὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτε εἰς οὐδὲν αὐτοῖς ἔστι χρήσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἀνάγκη κεῖσθαι διὰ τὸν ἐκ τοῦ χρόνου μαρασμὸν παραλυθέντος τοῦ τόνου. Ἡ ἐν γήρᾳ σωφροσύνη οὐ σωφροσύνη, ἀλλ' ἀκολασίας ἀδυναμία. Νεκρὸς οὐ στεφανοῦται· οὐδεὶς δίκαιος δι' ἀδυναμίαν κακοῦ. Ἕως ἔστι σοι δύναμις, λόγῳ κράτει τῆς ἁμαρτίας. Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ἀρετή· ἔκκλισις ἀπὸ κακοῦ, καὶ ποίησις ἀγαθοῦ. Ἡ δὲ ἀργία τῆς πονηρίας οὔτε ἐπαίνων αὐτὴ καθ' ἑαυτὴν, οὔτε κολάσεων ἀξιοῦται. Ἐὰν δι' ἡλι κίαν παύσῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, τῆς ἀσθενείας ἡ χάρις. Ἐπαινοῦμεν δὲ τοὺς κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἀγαθοὺς, οὐ τοὺς ἀπό τινος ἀνάγκης ἐξειργομένους.
thought_title: The hidden logic of delaying baptism
orientation: Basil is addressing the hearer who postpones baptism, exposing the unspoken reasoning behind the delay and answering it with warnings about sin, pleasure, and the danger of presuming on God's forgiveness.
pass_a_gloss: Do you, wretched one, lead pleasure as more honorable than so many and such great good things? For I understand your postponement, even if you cover it with words; the facts themselves shout, even if you are silent with your voice. Let me alone, let me use my flesh for the enjoyment of shameful things, let me wallow in the mire of pleasures, let me bloody my hands, let me take away what belongs to others, let me go deceitfully, let me swear falsely, let me lie; and then I will receive baptism, whenever I ever stop from evils. If then sin is good, keep it to the end; but if it is harmful to the one doing it, why do you remain in destructive things? No one, seeking to vomit bile, gathers more of it for himself from a wicked and dissolute way of life. It was fitting to cleanse the body of the things troubling it, not indeed to prepare a disease greater than one's power. The ship appears to bear the weight of cargo up to a certain point, but what is beyond this sinks it. Fear lest you also suffer similar things, and having made your sins greater than the forgiveness, you undergo shipwreck before the hoped-for harbors. Does God not see the things that happen? Or does he not understand your thoughts? Or does he work with you in your lawless deeds? You supposed lawlessness, he says, that I will be like you. But you, when you pursue the friendship of a mortal man, you bring him near through good deeds, saying and doing those things by which you perceive he rejoices; but when you are being made intimate with God, and hoping to be received into the rank of a son, you do the things hostile to God, and through transgression of the law you dishonor him, and from the very things by which you most offend, from these you hope for intimacy? See lest, on hope of redemption, having collected for yourself a multitude of evils, you gather sin together, but fail to obtain forgiveness. God is not mocked. Do not trade in the grace. Do not say: The law is good, but sin is sweeter. Pleasure is a hook of the devil, dragging to destruction. Pleasure is the mother of sin; and sin is the sting of death. Pleasure is the nurse of the eternal worm, which for a time softens the one enjoying it, but later makes its secretions more bitter than bile. The postponement shouts nothing other than these things: Let sin first reign in me, then the Lord will reign at some time. I will present my members as weapons of unrighteousness to lawlessness; then I will present them at some time also as weapons of righteousness to God. So also Cain offered the sacrifices: the first things to his own enjoyment, the second things to God who created and gave. When you are capable in deeds, you spend your youth on sins. When the instruments grow weary, then you bring them to God, when there is no use for them at all, but necessity lies there because of the withering from time, the tone having been slackened. Self-control in old age is not self-control, but inability for licentiousness. A corpse is not crowned; no one is righteous through inability to do evil. As long as there is power in you, master sin by reason. For this is virtue: turning away from evil, and doing good. But the idleness of wickedness is worthy neither of praises in itself, nor of punishments. If through age you stop from sin, the grace belongs to weakness. But we praise those who are good by choice, not those who are shut out by some necessity.

lemmas.gloss: mock, turn up the nose at

choices.why: Vocative address conveying Basil's direct, confrontational tone toward the delaying hearer; 'wretched' captures the moral misery implied.

The subjunctive expresses the imagined permission the hearer gives himself; 'use my flesh' keeps the bodily focus of σάρξ without importing 'sinful nature' here, since this is the hearer's own imagined speech about bodily indulgence.
rejected: let me make full use of the flesh

choices.english: let me wallow in the mire of pleasures
choices.why: The verb ἐγκυλίομαι means to roll or wallow in; 'mire' for βόρβορος conveys filth and degradation, matching Basil's vivid moral imagery.
rejected: let me roll in the mud of pleasures
let me be mired in pleasures

choices.english: Do not trade in the grace
choices.why: ἐμπορεύομαι means to engage in commerce; Basil warns against treating grace as a commodity to be bought or bargained with through delayed repentance.
rejected: Do not make merchandise of grace

choices.why: τροφός is a nurse or feeder; the image is that pleasure nourishes the worm that never dies, an allusion to the punishment of the wicked.
The genitive ἀκολασίας is objective: old age brings inability to practice licentiousness, not inability caused by licentiousness. 'Inability for' preserves this.

pass_b_english: Wretched one, do you really rank pleasure above goods so many and so great? I understand your postponement, even if you cover it over with words. The facts themselves cry out, even if your voice is silent. "Let me use my flesh for the enjoyment of shameful things; let me wallow in the mire of pleasures; let me stain my hands with blood, take what belongs to others, walk in deceit, swear falsely, lie—and then, when I finally stop doing evil, I will receive baptism." If sin is good, then keep it to the end. But if it harms the one who does it, why do you persist in what destroys you? No one who wants to vomit up bile first gathers more of it into himself through a bad and dissolute diet. You should cleanse the body of what troubles it, not make the disease greater than your strength. A ship shows how much weight of cargo it can bear; anything beyond that sinks it. Be afraid that you may suffer the same thing—that by making your sins greater than the forgiveness, you may suffer shipwreck before the hoped-for harbor. Does God not see what happens? Does He not understand your thoughts? Does He cooperate with you in your lawless deeds? You thought that I would be just like you, He says (Psalm 49:21). When you seek the friendship of a mortal man, you win him over with good deeds, saying and doing the things you know please him. But when you are drawing near to God and hoping to be received into the rank of a son, you do what is hostile to God and dishonor Him by breaking the law—and from the very things that most offend Him, you hope for closeness? Watch out: if you pile up a mass of evils for yourself in hope of redemption, you may gather sin and yet miss the forgiveness. God is not mocked (Galatians 6:7). Do not trade in the grace. Do not say, "The law is good, but sin is sweeter." Pleasure is the devil's fishhook, dragging you to destruction. Pleasure is the mother of sin, and sin is the sting of death (1 Corinthians 15:56). Pleasure is the nurse of the eternal worm: for a time it soothes the one who enjoys it, but afterward it produces a bitterness sharper than gall. Your postponement cries out nothing other than this: "Let sin reign in me first, and then one day the Lord will reign. Let me present my members as weapons of unrighteousness to lawlessness, and then one day I will present them as weapons of righteousness to God." That is how Cain offered his sacrifices: the first things to his own enjoyment, the second to God who created and gave them. While you are strong in deeds, you spend your youth on sins. When your organs are worn out, then you bring them to God—when they are good for nothing, when they must lie idle because their strength has been paralyzed by the decay of time. Self-control in old age is not self-control; it is inability for licentiousness. A corpse is not crowned. No one is righteous merely through being unable to do evil. As long as you have strength, master sin by your will. For this is virtue: turning away from evil and doing good. But mere inactivity in wickedness deserves neither praise nor punishment on its own. If you stop sinning because of age, the credit belongs to weakness. We praise those who are good by choice, not those who are kept from evil by some necessity.

problems.source_quote: Ὑπέλαβες ἀνομίαν, φησὶν, ὅτι ἔσομαί σοι ὅμοιος
problems.why: LXX Psalm 49:21, not Psalm 50:21. Hebrew numbering differs.
problems.ruling: LXX Psalm 49:21, not 50:21; Hebrew numbering differs from LXX.

fixed: Corrected Psalm 50:21 to Psalm 49:21; source is LXX Psalm 49:21 (Ὑπέλαβες ἀνομίαν, φησὶν, ὅτι ἔσομαί σοι ὅμοιος), which in Hebrew numbering is Psalm 49:21.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ὑπέλαβες ἀνομίαν, φησὶν, ὅτι ἔσομαί σοι ὅμοιος
last_rejected.why: LXX Psalm 49:21 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 50:21, not Psalm 49:21.
last_rejected.ruling: LXX Psalm 49:21 matches the Greek numbering used; the Hebrew 50:21 difference is standard, not an error.

last_rejected.quote: Does He cooperate with you in your lawless deeds?
last_rejected.why: This is a rhetorical question expecting 'no,' but the Greek syntax is difficult. However, συνεργάζεταί σοι τὰς ἀνομίας more naturally means 'Does He co-work/collaborate with you in your lawless deeds?' The English is essentially correct.
last_rejected.fix: Does He collaborate with you in your lawless deeds?
last_rejected.ruling: The reporter admits the English is essentially correct; no real error exists here.

last_rejected.quote: and then one day the Lord will reign
last_rejected.source_quote: εἶτα βασιλεύσει ποτὲ καὶ ὁ Κύριος
last_rejected.why: The English omits 'ποτὲ' ('one day/someday'), weakening the force of the procrastinator's 'someday' mentality that Basil is criticizing.
last_rejected.fix: and then one day the Lord too will reign
last_rejected.ruling: 'One day' appears in the next clause; 'ποτὲ' is adequately rendered without strict repetition.

last_rejected.why: ὄργανα here means 'bodily organs/members' in the sense of physical capacities/powers, but 'organs' in modern English strongly suggests internal organs (heart, liver, etc.). 'Limbs' or 'bodily powers' would be clearer.
last_rejected.ruling: 'ὄργανα' can mean bodily organs/members; 'organs' is within normal range, not a meaning change.
